name: Chicken Wings
blurb: The single most-cooked food in an air fryer. Rendered fat plus circulating heat gives you deep-fried crunch with no oil bath.
shake: Flip wings with tongs at 11 minutes so the side facing the basket floor can crisp.
internalNote: USDA safe minimum for all poultry, including wings, is 165°F. Check the thickest part of the drumette, avoiding bone.
prep: Pat completely dry with paper towels — surface moisture is the #1 reason wings come out rubbery. Toss with 1 tsp baking powder (not baking soda) per pound for extra blistering.
tips: Baking powder raises the skin's pH so proteins brown faster — this is the restaurant trick for shatter-crisp skin.
Sauce AFTER cooking, never before. Sugary sauces burn at 400°F and glue wings to the basket.
Single layer only. Stacked wings steam each other and you'll get pale, floppy skin.
ingredients: 1 lb chicken wings, split into flats and drums
steps: Pat wings bone-dry and toss with baking powder, salt, pepper and garlic powder.
Arrange in a single layer in the basket, skin side up, with space between each piece.
Cook at 400°F for 11 minutes.
Flip each wing and cook another 11 minutes until deep golden and 165°F internal.
Rest 3 minutes, then toss in sauce and serve immediately.

faq.q: Do I need to thaw frozen wings first?
faq.a: No. Cook them straight from frozen at 400°F for about 28 minutes, separating them with tongs at the 8-minute mark once the ice releases. Add 2-3 minutes if they were frozen in a solid block.

faq.q: Why are my wings not crispy?
faq.a: Almost always moisture or crowding. Dry the wings thoroughly, use baking powder, and cook no more than a single uncrowded layer at a time.

name: Chicken Breast
blurb: Boneless chicken breast is easy to overcook. The air fryer's short, hot cycle actually helps — less time on heat means less moisture loss.
shake: Flip once at 10 minutes. Don't flip more — every open cycle drops the chamber temperature.
internalNote: 165°F in the thickest part. Pull at 162°F and let carryover heat finish it during the rest — this is the difference between juicy and chalky.
prep: Pound to an even 3/4-inch thickness so the thin end doesn't dry out while the thick end catches up. A 30-minute brine in 4 cups water + 1/4 cup salt is transformative.
tips: Even thickness matters more than time. A tapered breast will always overcook at one end.
Rest 5 minutes before slicing. Cutting immediately dumps the juices onto your board.
A light coat of oil helps seasoning stick and prevents the surface from turning leathery.
ingredients: 2 boneless skinless chicken breasts (6-8 oz each)
steps: Pound breasts to even thickness and pat dry.
Rub with oil, then coat with combined spices.
Place in a single layer, not touching.
Cook at 375°F for 10 minutes, flip, then 8 more minutes.
Verify 165°F with a thermometer and rest 5 minutes before slicing.

faq.q: Can I cook chicken breast from frozen?
faq.a: Yes — 360°F for roughly 28 minutes, flipping at 15. The lower temperature gives the center time to reach 165°F before the outside dries out. Always confirm with a thermometer.

faq.q: Should I preheat for chicken breast?
faq.a: Yes. A 3-minute preheat sears the surface on contact, which locks in noticeably more moisture than starting in a cold basket.

name: Chicken Thighs
keywords: bone in chicken thighs air fryer
blurb: Forgiving, fatty, and nearly impossible to ruin. Bone-in skin-on thighs are the best value cut for air frying.
shake: Start skin-side down, flip skin-side up at 15 minutes for the final crisping stretch.
internalNote: 165°F is the safe minimum, but thighs are better at 175-180°F — the extra time melts connective tissue without drying the meat.
prep: Trim excess flaps of skin and fat, which can smoke. Season under the skin as well as on top.
tips: Thighs render a lot of fat — add a tablespoon of water to the drawer beneath the basket to stop smoke.
Unlike breast, thighs benefit from going past 165°F. Aim for 175°F for silky texture.
Skin-side down first, then flip: the rendered fat drains and the skin crisps in its own fat.
steps: Pat thighs dry and trim excess fat.
Rub oil and spices over and under the skin.
Place skin-side down in the basket.
Cook at 380°F for 15 minutes.
Flip skin-side up and cook 10 more minutes until skin is crackling and internal temp reads 175°F.

faq.a: Boneless skinless thighs need about 18 minutes at 380°F. Bone-in takes 25 because the bone slows heat transfer to the center.

faq.q: Why is my air fryer smoking with thighs?
faq.a: Rendered chicken fat hitting the hot heating element. Pour a tablespoon or two of water into the outer drawer, or line beneath the basket with a small piece of foil that doesn't block airflow.

name: Chicken Drumsticks
blurb: Cheap, kid-friendly, and they cook more evenly than you'd expect because the meat wraps a single straight bone.
shake: Turn each drumstick a half-rotation at 12 minutes.
internalNote: 165°F minimum measured against — not touching — the bone. Dark meat is more pleasant at 175°F.
prep: Dry the skin well and season aggressively; drumsticks have a high skin-to-meat ratio so surface seasoning carries the whole dish.
tips: Stand them upright leaning against the basket wall if you're cooking six — more airflow, same footprint.
A 10-minute dry brine with salt draws moisture out then reabsorbs it, seasoning the meat deeper.
Brush with BBQ sauce only in the last 3 minutes to prevent burning.
steps: Pat drumsticks dry and rub with oil.
Combine dry seasonings and coat evenly.
Arrange in a single layer with space between.
Cook at 390°F for 12 minutes, turn, then 10 minutes more.
Check for 165°F minimum and rest 3 minutes.

faq.a: Only if you shake and rearrange every 8 minutes, and add about 5 minutes total. A single layer is meaningfully crispier.
A light coat helps seasoning adhere and speeds browning, but the skin has enough fat to crisp on its own if you're avoiding added oil.

name: Frozen Chicken Nuggets
blurb: The fastest weeknight win there is. Frozen nuggets go from freezer to plate in ten minutes and come out crunchier than the oven ever managed.
shake: Shake the basket firmly at 5 minutes so the nuggets tumble and brown on all sides.
internalNote: Frozen nuggets are pre-cooked but must be reheated to 165°F throughout. Cut one open — steam should escape and there should be no cold center.
prep: No thawing, no oil, no preheat needed for most models. Just dump and shake.
tips: No oil spray required — frozen nuggets are already par-fried and carry their own fat.
Two layers is fine here if you shake twice; nuggets are small enough that airflow still reaches them.
Add 2 minutes if you like them properly crunchy rather than just heated.
steps: Pour nuggets into the basket, spreading roughly level.
Cook at 380°F for 5 minutes.
Shake the basket vigorously.
Cook 5 more minutes until golden and hot through.
Serve immediately — they lose crunch fast as they cool.

faq.q: Do I need to preheat for nuggets?
faq.a: Not really. Frozen nuggets are forgiving; skipping preheat costs you maybe a minute. Preheat if you want maximum crunch.

faq.q: What temperature for homemade breaded nuggets?
faq.a: 380°F for about 8 minutes, flipping once. Spray the breading lightly with oil so the flour turns golden instead of powdery white.

name: Chicken Tenders
blurb: Breaded tenders are where the air fryer genuinely beats deep frying on convenience — same crunch, no pot of oil to dispose of.
shake: Flip each tender at 6 minutes with tongs — shaking can knock breading loose.
internalNote: 165°F. Tenders are thin, so they hit temp fast; check the thickest one at the earliest time.
prep: For homemade: flour, then egg, then panko. Press the panko on firmly and let the breaded tenders sit 10 minutes so the coating hydrates and clings.
tips: Spray the breading with oil until no dry white flour spots remain — dry spots stay dry and taste raw.
Panko outperforms standard breadcrumbs in an air fryer; the larger flakes catch more air.
Use tongs, not a shake, or you'll strip the coating off.
steps: Season flour with paprika, garlic powder and salt.
Dredge each tender in flour, then egg, then press firmly into panko.
Rest breaded tenders 10 minutes on a rack.
Spray both sides with oil and arrange in a single layer.
Cook at 380°F for 6 minutes, flip, spray again, and cook 6 more minutes to 165°F.

faq.q: Why does my breading fall off?
faq.a: Usually wet chicken or skipping the rest. Pat the tenders dry before flouring, press the panko on hard, and let them sit 10 minutes before cooking.
390°F for 14 minutes, flipping at 7. No oil spray needed — they're already par-fried.

name: Whole Roast Chicken
blurb: A whole bird in under an hour with skin that beats any oven roast. You need a 5.8-quart basket or larger.
shake: Start breast-side down, flip breast-side up at 30 minutes.
internalNote: 165°F in the thickest part of the thigh, not touching bone. The breast will read slightly higher — that's fine.
prep: Remove giblets, truss the legs with kitchen twine, and tuck the wing tips under so nothing burns against the element.
tips: Breast-down first uses gravity to baste the breast in thigh fat, then you flip to crisp the skin.
Dry-brine uncovered in the fridge overnight for the crispiest possible skin.
Measure your basket first — a 4 lb bird needs roughly 5.8 qt of clearance, and it must not touch the heating element.
steps: Remove giblets, pat the bird completely dry, and truss the legs.
Rub all over with oil and the combined seasoning, including inside the cavity.
Place breast-side down in the basket.
Cook at 350°F for 30 minutes.
Flip breast-side up and cook 25 more minutes until the thigh reads 165°F.
Rest 10 minutes before carving — this is not optional for a whole bird.

faq.q: What size chicken fits in an air fryer?
faq.a: Up to about 4 lb in a 5.8-quart basket, or 5 lb in a 7-quart or oven-style model. The bird must have at least an inch of clearance from the heating element.
Roughly 14-15 minutes per pound at 350°F, but always finish by thermometer rather than by the clock.

name: Turkey Breast
keywords: bone in turkey breast air fryer
blurb: A 3-pound turkey breast in 45 minutes frees up your oven on Thanksgiving and produces better skin than a full roast.
shake: Start skin-side down, flip skin-side up at 25 minutes.
internalNote: 165°F at the thickest point. Turkey breast is very lean — even 5 degrees over makes a noticeable difference.
prep: Thaw completely — never air fry a frozen turkey breast. Dry-brine with salt 12-24 hours ahead if you can.
tips: Loosely tent with foil if the skin darkens before the center is done.
Butter under the skin bastes the lean meat as it renders.
Rest a full 15 minutes. A large piece of meat continues cooking 5-8 degrees after you pull it.
steps: Pat the breast dry and loosen the skin with your fingers.
Spread butter under the skin, then rub seasoning over the surface.
Place skin-side down in the basket.
Cook at 350°F for 25 minutes.
Flip skin-side up and cook 20 more minutes to 165°F.
Rest 15 minutes, tented loosely, before slicing.

faq.q: Can I cook a frozen turkey breast?
faq.a: No. A piece this dense will still be frozen at the core long after the exterior is overcooked, which is a real food-safety risk. Thaw in the fridge for 24 hours per 4-5 lb.
About 35 minutes at 350°F for a 3 lb boneless roast, flipping halfway. It cooks faster without the bone.

name: Bacon
blurb: No splatter, no standing over a pan, and the fat drains away. The air fryer's best breakfast trick.
shake: Flip strips at 5 minutes and rearrange any that have curled together.
internalNote: No thermometer needed — bacon is done when it reaches the color and rigidity you like. Cured pork is safe once heated through.
prep: Cut strips in half so they lie flat. Curled bacon cooks unevenly and touches the element.
tips: Add 2 tablespoons of water to the drawer under the basket — it stops rendered fat from smoking, which is the #1 bacon complaint.
350°F, not 400°F. Bacon fat starts smoking hard above 375°F.
Thick-cut needs 12-13 minutes; center-cut needs 7-8. Check at the low end.
steps: Pour 2 tbsp water into the drawer beneath the basket to control smoke.
Lay bacon in a single layer, slight overlap is fine as it shrinks.
Cook at 350°F for 5 minutes.
Flip and separate strips, then cook 4 more minutes.
Drain on paper towels — it crisps further as it cools.

faq.q: Why does my air fryer smoke when cooking bacon?
faq.a: Rendered fat pooling under the basket and hitting the hot element. Two tablespoons of water in the drawer solves it completely.
Yes, at 350°F for about 12 minutes. Cook 3 minutes first, then pry the strips apart with tongs once they loosen.

name: Pork Chops
blurb: Modern pork is bred lean, so the old 'cook until white' advice ruins it. 145°F and a rest gives you a chop that's actually juicy.
shake: Flip once at 6 minutes.
internalNote: USDA lowered pork to 145°F with a 3-minute rest in 2011. A faint blush of pink at 145°F is safe and expected.
prep: Bring chops to room temperature for 20 minutes and pat dry. A cold chop from the fridge cooks unevenly.
tips: 145°F plus a 3-minute rest — this is the USDA standard and it's a completely different eating experience from the old 160°F rule.
Bone-in chops take 2-3 minutes longer but stay juicier.
A quick brine (1/4 cup salt in 4 cups water, 30 minutes) is the cheapest upgrade available.
steps: Bring chops to room temp and pat dry.
Rub with oil and the combined seasoning.
Arrange in a single layer, not touching.
Cook at 380°F for 6 minutes, flip, then 6 minutes more.
Pull at 145°F and rest 3 minutes before serving.

faq.a: Yes, at 145°F internal with a 3-minute rest. The USDA revised this guidance in 2011; a slight pink tint in properly cooked pork is normal.
Half-inch chops need only about 8 minutes total at 380°F, flipping at 4. They overcook very quickly.

name: Pork Tenderloin
blurb: An entire dinner protein in 20 minutes. Tenderloin is uniform in shape, which is exactly what an air fryer handles best.
shake: Rotate a quarter-turn at 10 minutes to brown all four sides.
internalNote: 145°F with a 3-minute rest. Tenderloin is extremely lean — past 150°F it turns dry and grainy fast.
prep: Remove the silverskin, the shiny membrane along one side. It doesn't break down and will make the meat curl as it tightens.
tips: Cut it in half if it doesn't fit — two shorter pieces cook the same as one long one.
Silverskin removal takes 60 seconds and dramatically improves texture.
Rest 5 minutes then slice into medallions across the grain.
steps: Trim silverskin and pat dry.
Rub with oil and mustard, then coat in the seasoning blend.
Place diagonally in the basket, halving it if needed.
Cook at 400°F for 10 minutes.
Rotate and cook 10 more minutes to 145°F.
Rest 5 minutes, then slice into 1/2-inch medallions.

faq.q: Tenderloin vs pork loin — same thing?
faq.a: No, and it matters. Tenderloin is a small 1 lb muscle that cooks in 20 minutes. Pork loin is a wide 3-4 lb roast needing about 45 minutes at 350°F.
Not necessary. At 400°F the air fryer browns the exterior on its own within the cook time.

name: Steak
blurb: You won't get a cast-iron crust, but you will get edge-to-edge even doneness with zero smoke alarms — a genuinely good trade in an apartment.
shake: Flip once at 5 minutes. A single flip gives you the best crust.
internalNote: USDA recommends 145°F with a 3-minute rest for whole cuts of beef. For personal preference: 130-135°F medium-rare, 140°F medium, 150°F medium-well — these are below the USDA minimum and carry slightly higher risk.
prep: Salt the steak and leave it uncovered in the fridge for at least 45 minutes. A dry surface is the only way to get browning.
tips: Preheat the air fryer fully for 5 minutes — going into a hot chamber is what forms the crust.
Never cook two steaks touching. The gap between them is where the browning air travels.
A 60-second finish in a hot buttered skillet after air frying gives you the best of both methods.
ingredients: 1 ribeye or NY strip steak, 1-inch thick
steps: Salt the steak and rest uncovered in the fridge 45 minutes; pat dry.
Preheat air fryer to 400°F for 5 minutes.
Rub steak with oil and pepper, place in the hot basket.
Cook 5 minutes, flip, then 5 minutes for medium-rare (130-135°F).
Rest 5 minutes, topped with butter and smashed garlic.

faq.q: Can I cook a frozen steak?
faq.a: Yes — 360°F for about 20 minutes, flipping at 10. It won't crust as well, but the interior comes out surprisingly even because the frozen core resists overcooking.

faq.q: How do I get a better crust?
faq.a: Dry surface, full preheat, and no crowding. For a real hard sear, finish the steak for 45-60 seconds per side in a screaming-hot skillet with butter.

name: Hamburgers
blurb: Ground beef needs to hit 160°F, which is exactly where burgers usually turn into hockey pucks. The air fryer's fast cycle keeps them juicy at temp.
shake: Flip at 6 minutes with a thin spatula.
internalNote: 160°F for all ground beef — no exceptions. Grinding distributes surface bacteria throughout the patty, so the whole thing must reach temp.
prep: Press a shallow dimple into the center of each raw patty. It stops the burger from doming into a meatball as the proteins contract.
tips: 80/20 ground beef is the right ratio. Anything leaner dries out before it reaches 160°F.
Add cheese in the final 60 seconds with the basket closed — it melts perfectly in the residual heat.
Don't press the patty while cooking. You're squeezing out the fat that makes it good.
steps: Divide beef into two loose patties, slightly wider than your buns.
Dimple the center of each and season both sides.
Place in the basket with space between them.
Cook at 375°F for 6 minutes, flip, then 6 minutes to 160°F.
Add cheese for the last minute, then rest 2 minutes before assembling.

faq.a: Yes. 375°F for about 16 minutes, flipping at 8. Season after the surface thaws at around 4 minutes so the seasoning sticks.

faq.q: Do burgers make a mess in the air fryer?
faq.a: Some fat drips. Add a tablespoon of water to the drawer below the basket to prevent smoking, and clean the basket while it's still warm.

name: Meatballs
blurb: Round food and circulating air are a perfect match. Meatballs brown on every surface without you turning a single one in a skillet.
shake: Shake the basket at 6 minutes — they'll roll and expose new surfaces.
internalNote: 160°F for beef or pork meatballs; 165°F if they contain ground chicken or turkey.
prep: Mix gently with wet hands. Overworked ground meat turns dense and springy rather than tender.
tips: A panade — bread soaked in milk — is what keeps meatballs moist. Don't skip it.
Roll them uniform in size so they finish together; an ice cream scoop makes this easy.
Frozen pre-cooked meatballs just need reheating to 165°F, roughly 8 minutes.
steps: Soak breadcrumbs in milk for 5 minutes to form a panade.
Combine all ingredients, mixing gently with wet hands.
Roll into 16 even 1.5-inch balls.
Arrange in a single layer with space between.
Cook at 380°F for 6 minutes, shake, then 5 more minutes to 160°F.

faq.q: Frozen raw vs frozen cooked meatballs?
faq.a: Frozen raw need 14 minutes at 380°F to reach 160°F. Frozen pre-cooked only need reheating — about 8 minutes to 165°F.

faq.q: Can I cook them in sauce?
faq.a: Not in the basket. Air fry them dry first, then transfer to simmering sauce. Sauce in the basket blocks airflow and makes a mess.

name: Salmon Fillet
blurb: Ten minutes, no fishy kitchen smell lingering for two days, and the skin turns to a crisp chip. Salmon may be the air fryer's best result overall.
shake: No flip needed. Salmon is delicate and turning it usually breaks the fillet apart.
internalNote: USDA says 145°F, at which point the flesh flakes easily. Many cooks prefer 125-130°F for a silkier center, which is below the USDA minimum.
prep: Pat the skin bone-dry and salt it 10 minutes ahead. Wet skin steams; dry skin crisps.
tips: Skin-side down the whole time — the skin acts as insulation and protects the flesh from the direct heat below.
Thickness governs time, not weight. A 1-inch fillet needs 9 minutes; a thin tail piece needs 6.
White albumin seeping out means it's overcooking. Pull it earlier next time.
ingredients: 2 salmon fillets, 6 oz each, skin on
steps: Pat fillets completely dry, especially the skin.
Rub with oil and season the flesh side.
Place skin-side down in the basket, not touching.
Cook at 390°F for 9 minutes without flipping.
Check that it flakes with a fork at 145°F; serve with lemon and dill.

faq.q: Can I cook salmon from frozen?
faq.a: Yes, and it works well. 375°F for about 14 minutes. Cook 5 minutes first, then season once the surface thaws enough for it to stick.
Air fryer salmon skin gets genuinely crispy and is the best part. If you don't want it, the cooked fillet lifts cleanly off the skin with a spatula.

name: Shrimp
blurb: Six minutes, start to finish. Shrimp is the fastest protein in the air fryer and the easiest to ruin by walking away.
shake: Shake at 3 minutes. With a 6-minute cook, that single shake matters a lot.
internalNote: 145°F, but visual cues are more practical: shrimp are done when opaque and curled into a loose C. A tight O means overcooked.
prep: Thaw and dry thoroughly. Wet shrimp release water and poach themselves instead of roasting.
tips: A loose C shape is perfect. A tight O is rubbery. This is the most useful doneness cue in cooking.
Set a timer — the window between perfect and ruined is under 90 seconds.
Larger shrimp are more forgiving. Jumbo 16-20 count gives you more margin for error.
ingredients: 1 lb large shrimp, peeled and deveined
steps: Thaw shrimp fully and pat very dry.
Toss with oil, garlic, paprika, salt and pepper flakes.
Spread in a single layer in the basket.
Cook at 400°F for 3 minutes, shake, then 3 minutes more.
Pull the moment they're opaque and C-shaped; finish with lemon juice.

faq.q: Can I cook shrimp from frozen?
faq.a: Yes — 400°F for about 9 minutes. Rinse off ice glaze and dry them first, or they'll steam. Shake twice during cooking.
375°F for 8 minutes, flipping at 4. Spray with oil so the coconut toasts golden instead of drying out white.

name: Breaded Fish Fillets
blurb: Fish and chips without the deep fryer. Frozen battered fillets in particular come out dramatically better than from an oven.
shake: Flip carefully with a thin spatula at 6 minutes — fish breaks easily.
internalNote: 145°F, or until the fish flakes cleanly with a fork and is opaque all the way through.
prep: For fresh fish: flour, egg, then panko. Cod, haddock and pollock all work; avoid very thin fillets like sole, which fall apart.
tips: Frozen battered fillets need no oil and no thawing — this is the single easiest air fryer meal.
Line up fillets in one layer with a finger-width gap; touching fillets fuse together.
A wire rack or perforated parchment stops delicate fillets sticking to the basket.
steps: Cut fish into even 4-6 oz portions and pat dry.
Dredge in seasoned flour, then egg, then panko, pressing firmly.
Spray both sides with oil.
Arrange in a single layer without touching.
Cook at 390°F for 6 minutes, flip gently, then 6 minutes more to 145°F.

faq.a: 400°F for 9-10 minutes, shaking at 5. They're smaller than full fillets so they cook faster.

faq.q: Why did my fish stick to the basket?
faq.a: Delicate fish grips bare metal. Use perforated parchment, a light oil spray on the basket, or a wire rack insert.

name: Frozen French Fries
blurb: The reason most people buy an air fryer. Frozen fries come out closer to fast-food quality than any oven can manage.
shake: Shake twice — at 6 and 11 minutes. Fries stick to each other more than any other food.
internalNote: No internal temp needed. Fries are done when the outside is golden and rigid and the inside is fluffy.
prep: Straight from the freezer. Never thaw fries — thawed potato goes limp and soggy.
tips: Two shakes minimum. Fries clump and the clumped faces stay pale.
Cook no more than a 1.5-inch deep layer. Beyond that, the top browns and the bottom steams.
No oil needed for most frozen fries; they're par-fried already. A light spray helps thin shoestring cuts.
steps: Pour fries into the basket straight from the freezer.
Cook at 400°F for 6 minutes.
Shake vigorously and cook 5 more minutes.
Shake again and cook a final 5 minutes until deep golden.
Salt immediately while hot so it sticks.

faq.q: Do I need to preheat for frozen fries?
faq.a: A 3-minute preheat gives measurably crispier results because the fries hit hot metal immediately instead of warming up slowly with the chamber.
Overcrowding, almost always. Halve the batch. Also make sure you never thaw them first.

name: Sweet Potato Fries
blurb: Sweet potatoes have more sugar and moisture than russets, so they burn and sag more easily. Cornstarch and a lower temperature fix both problems.
shake: Shake at 8 minutes and separate any that have fused.
internalNote: Done by texture: crisp edges, tender centers. Sweet potato needs to cook through or it stays starchy.
prep: Soak cut fries in cold water 30 minutes to leach surface starch, then dry completely. This is the step everyone skips and it's the one that matters.
tips: One tablespoon of cornstarch per pound creates a thin shell that turns genuinely crispy.
380°F, not 400°F. Sweet potato sugars scorch before the inside softens at higher heat.
Cut into uniform 1/4-inch batons. Thick-cut wedges will never crisp the same way.
ingredients: 2 medium sweet potatoes, cut into 1/4-inch fries
steps: Soak the cut fries in cold water for 30 minutes, then dry completely with towels.
Toss with cornstarch until evenly dusted.
Add oil and seasonings and toss again.
Cook at 380°F for 8 minutes in a single layer.
Shake and cook 8 more minutes until edges are crisp.

faq.q: Why won't my sweet potato fries get crispy?
faq.a: Excess moisture and no starch coating. Soak, dry thoroughly, and use cornstarch. Also cook in two batches rather than one crowded one.
400°F for 15 minutes, shaking twice. Frozen ones are pre-treated and crisp more reliably than homemade.

name: Tater Tots
blurb: Tots are engineered for hot circulating air. They come out uniformly bronzed with a crackly shell every single time.
shake: Shake once at 7 minutes.
internalNote: Done when uniformly golden brown and firm to a tong squeeze.
prep: No prep at all. Straight from the bag.
tips: Tots tolerate a slightly deeper layer than fries because their shape leaves natural air gaps.
Add 2 minutes if you want them shatteringly crisp rather than just cooked.
Cheese and toppings go on in the last 2 minutes, not before.
steps: Add tots to the basket in a roughly even layer.
Cook at 400°F for 7 minutes.
Shake the basket well.
Cook 7 more minutes until deep golden.
Season and serve hot.

faq.q: Can I make a tot casserole in the air fryer?
faq.a: Use a small oven-safe dish inside the basket for cheese-topped tots. Airflow drops with a solid dish, so add about 4 minutes.
Optional but helpful. Three minutes of preheat gives a crisper exterior.

name: Onion Rings
blurb: Frozen onion rings crisp beautifully. Homemade battered ones are trickier — the air fryer can't set a wet batter the way hot oil does.
shake: Flip with tongs at 5 minutes rather than shaking; rings break.
internalNote: Golden brown and crisp; the onion inside should be soft and translucent.
prep: For homemade, use a dry breading — flour, egg, panko — not a wet beer batter. Wet batter drips through the basket before it sets.
tips: Frozen rings need no oil. Homemade breaded ones need a generous oil spray or the flour tastes raw.
Single layer, no overlap. Overlapping rings weld together.
Wet batters do not work in an air fryer. Use a breaded coating instead.
ingredients: 1 lb frozen onion rings, or 2 large onions plus breading
steps: Arrange rings in a single layer, standing some against the basket wall if needed.
Cook at 400°F for 5 minutes.
Flip each ring with tongs.
Cook 5 more minutes until golden and crisp.

faq.a: No. Wet batter drips off before it sets and makes a mess of the drawer. Use flour, egg wash, and panko instead.
380°F for 12 minutes, flipping at 6, with a solid oil spray on both sides.

name: Mozzarella Sticks
blurb: High reward, low margin for error. Thirty seconds too long and you have a puddle of cheese and an empty breadcrumb shell.
shake: Flip gently with tongs at 4 minutes.
internalNote: Done when the coating is golden and the cheese is just molten. Do not wait for cheese to visibly bubble out — that's already too far.
prep: Keep them frozen solid until the second they go in. Any thawing guarantees a blowout.
tips: Set a timer and watch the last 2 minutes. This food genuinely does not forgive inattention.
Never thaw. Frozen-solid cheese is what buys you time for the coating to brown.
Leave gaps between sticks — cheese that leaks will glue neighbors together.
steps: Place frozen sticks in a single layer with space between them.
Cook at 390°F for 4 minutes.
Flip carefully with tongs.
Cook 3 more minutes, checking at 2.
Remove the instant the coating is golden; rest 1 minute before serving.

faq.q: Why did my cheese explode out?
faq.a: Too long, too hot, or partially thawed. Drop to 380°F, cut a minute, and cook straight from a solid freeze.

faq.q: Can I make them from scratch?
faq.a: Yes, but double-bread them and freeze the breaded sticks for at least 2 hours before cooking. Single-breaded fresh cheese will always burst.

name: Frozen Pizza
blurb: A crisper base than any oven produces, in a third of the time — as long as the pizza physically fits your basket.
shake: No flip or shake. Rotate the pizza 180° at 5 minutes if your model browns unevenly.
internalNote: Done when the cheese is fully melted with a few browned spots and the crust edge is firm.
prep: Measure your basket before you buy. Most baskets take a 7-8 inch pizza; oven-style models handle 9-10 inches.
tips: Cook straight from frozen — a thawed frozen pizza goes soggy in the middle.
If cheese starts to fly around from the fan, place a toothpick through the center of the pizza to pin it down.
Watch the crust edge, not the clock. Thin crust can finish 2 minutes early.
steps: Remove all packaging and any cardboard disc.
Place the frozen pizza directly in the basket.
Cook at 375°F for 5 minutes.
Check and rotate if browning unevenly, then cook 4 more minutes.
Rest 2 minutes before slicing so the cheese sets.

faq.q: What if my pizza doesn't fit?
faq.a: Cut it into quarters and cook two at a time, or use French bread and pita as a base instead. Never force a pizza to curl up the basket wall.
Yes, and it's the best method there is. 350°F for 3-4 minutes restores a crisp base — a microwave never will.

name: Brussels Sprouts
blurb: The vegetable that converts skeptics. Air frying caramelizes the outer leaves into something closer to a chip than a boiled sprout.
shake: Shake hard at 8 minutes. The loose outer leaves that fall off become the best part.
internalNote: Done when a knife slides into the core with no resistance and the outer leaves are dark and crisp.
prep: Halve them through the stem and trim the dry base. Cut-side down for the first half of cooking gives you a caramelized flat face.
tips: Cut-side down first — that flat surface against hot metal is where the deep browning happens.
Don't rescue the loose leaves that fall off. They turn into crisps and everyone fights over them.
A drizzle of balsamic or honey in the last 2 minutes glazes without burning.
steps: Trim and halve sprouts through the stem.
Toss with oil, salt, pepper and garlic.
Arrange cut-side down in a single layer.
Cook at 380°F for 8 minutes.
Shake and cook 7 more minutes until browned and tender.
Finish with balsamic if using.

faq.a: They work but won't get as crisp because of ice content. 380°F for 18 minutes, shaking twice, and don't thaw first.
Undercooking. Bitterness breaks down with caramelization — push them 3-4 minutes further than feels right.

name: Broccoli
blurb: Charred tips, tender stems, eight minutes. Just be aware that dry florets can scorch — a little oil is genuinely required here.
shake: Shake at 5 minutes so the top florets swap places with the bottom ones.
internalNote: Done when stems are fork-tender and floret tips are browned and slightly crisp.
prep: Cut into even florets with some flat surface. Toss with oil thoroughly — unoiled floret tips burn to ash while stems stay raw.
tips: Broccoli must be oiled. The delicate tips carbonize without a fat coating.
Cut florets no larger than 1.5 inches, or the stem won't cook through before the top burns.
Parmesan and lemon zest in the final minute is the standard finish for a reason.
ingredients: 1 large head broccoli, cut into florets
steps: Cut broccoli into even 1.5-inch florets.
Toss thoroughly with oil until every tip is coated.
Season with salt, garlic powder and pepper flakes.
Cook at 375°F for 5 minutes, shake, then 4 minutes more.
Toss with Parmesan and lemon zest off the heat.

faq.q: Frozen broccoli in the air fryer?
faq.a: Yes — 375°F for 13 minutes, no thawing. It'll be softer than fresh because of ice, but the tips still brown.
Not enough oil, or florets cut too small. Toss until visibly glossy and keep pieces at least an inch across.

name: Baby Potatoes
blurb: Crackly skin, creamy interior. Air-fried baby potatoes are one of the few side dishes that genuinely improve on the oven version.
shake: Shake at 10 minutes and again at 15 if you're cooking a full basket.
internalNote: Done when a knife or skewer slides through with no resistance and the skin is blistered.
prep: Halve anything bigger than a golf ball. A 5-minute par-boil before air frying gives you the fluffiest possible interior.
tips: Par-boiling for 5 minutes then roughing them up in the colander creates edges that fry into crunchy shards.
Halve them cut-side down for a caramelized flat face.
Add fresh herbs like rosemary at the end, not the start — they burn at 390°F.
steps: Halve potatoes and optionally par-boil 5 minutes, then drain and dry.
Toss with oil, salt, pepper, garlic powder and rosemary.
Arrange cut-side down in a single layer.
Cook at 390°F for 10 minutes.
Shake and cook 10 more minutes until crisp and fork-tender.
Toss with parsley before serving.

faq.q: Whole baked potato in the air fryer?
faq.a: Yes. A large russet takes about 40 minutes at 390°F. Pierce it several times, rub with oil and salt, and turn once at 20 minutes.
No, but it produces a noticeably fluffier interior and crispier crust. Skip it on a weeknight, do it for guests.

name: Asparagus
blurb: Seven minutes from raw to blistered. Asparagus is the fastest vegetable in the machine and the hardest to overcook badly.
shake: Shake or roll the spears at 4 minutes.
internalNote: Done when spears bend slightly under their own weight but still snap when bitten.
prep: Snap off the woody ends — hold each spear and bend until it breaks naturally at the tender point.
tips: Thick spears take 9 minutes, pencil-thin ones only 5. Sort by thickness before cooking.
Lay them perpendicular to the basket slots so none fall through.
Parmesan and lemon added off-heat prevents the cheese from scorching.
steps: Snap off woody ends and dry the spears.
Toss with oil, salt and pepper.
Lay in a single layer across the basket slots.
Cook at 390°F for 4 minutes, shake, then 3 more.
Finish with Parmesan and a squeeze of lemon.

faq.a: 390°F for about 11 minutes. It comes out softer than fresh — frozen asparagus has already had its cell walls ruptured by ice.

faq.q: How do I stop thin spears burning?
faq.a: Cut 2 minutes off and check at 5. Very thin asparagus cooks nearly twice as fast as thick spears.

name: Cauliflower
blurb: Air frying turns cauliflower nutty and golden instead of the watery blandness you get from steaming.
shake: Shake at 7 minutes to rotate the browned faces.
internalNote: Done when edges are deeply golden and a knife enters the stem easily.
prep: Cut florets so each has one flat cut face. Flat faces are where browning happens.
tips: Cauliflower absorbs oil quickly — measure it rather than pouring, or it turns greasy.
For buffalo cauliflower, sauce it in the last 3 minutes only.
Turmeric or curry powder is especially good here; cauliflower is bland enough to take strong spice.
steps: Cut cauliflower into even florets with flat faces.
Toss with oil and all seasonings.
Spread in a single layer, flat sides down.
Cook at 390°F for 7 minutes.
Shake and cook 7 more minutes until browned at the edges.

faq.a: 390°F for 18 minutes, shaking twice. Expect softer texture than fresh — there's no way around the ice content.

faq.q: How do I make buffalo cauliflower?
faq.a: Air fry plain for 11 minutes, toss in buffalo sauce, then return for 3 more minutes to set the glaze.

name: Zucchini
blurb: Zucchini is 95% water, which is exactly why most people end up with mush. Salting first is mandatory, not optional.
shake: Shake at 6 minutes, gently — cooked zucchini falls apart.
internalNote: Done when edges are browned and slices are tender but still hold their shape.
prep: Slice into 1/2-inch rounds or spears, salt them, and let them drain in a colander 15 minutes. Then press dry with towels. This removes surprising amounts of water.
tips: Salt-and-drain first. Skipping it is the entire reason zucchini turns to mush.
Cut thick — 1/2-inch minimum. Thin slices have no structure left after cooking.
400°F drives water off fast. Lower temperatures just steam it.
steps: Slice zucchini, toss with 1 tsp salt, and drain in a colander 15 minutes.
Press slices dry between paper towels.
Toss with oil, Italian seasoning and garlic powder.
Cook at 400°F for 6 minutes, shake, then 6 more.
Finish with Parmesan and pepper.

faq.a: You skipped the salt-and-drain step, or cut it too thin. Both are fixable — salt for 15 minutes and cut at least 1/2-inch thick.
Yes. Salt and dry first, then flour, egg and panko. Cook at 400°F for 10 minutes, flipping once, with an oil spray.

name: Green Beans
blurb: Blistered, snappy, and done in eight minutes — closer to restaurant blistered beans than to the soft ones from a pot.
shake: Shake at 4 minutes.
internalNote: Done when beans are blistered in spots and snap rather than bend.
prep: Trim the stem ends and dry thoroughly after washing.
tips: Wet beans steam instead of blistering — dry them properly after washing.
Garlic added at the start burns; add minced garlic in the last 2 minutes.
Frozen green beans work, but expect limp texture rather than snap.
steps: Trim and thoroughly dry the beans.
Toss with oil, salt and pepper.
Spread in the basket in a loose layer.
Cook at 375°F for 4 minutes, shake, then 3 minutes.
Add garlic and almonds for the final minute; finish with lemon zest.

faq.a: 375°F for 12 minutes, shaking twice. Don't thaw — go straight from frozen and accept a softer result.

faq.q: Can I make green bean fries?
faq.a: Yes. Bread them in flour, egg and panko, spray with oil, and cook at 390°F for 9 minutes, flipping once.

name: Corn on the Cob
keywords: air fryer corn on the cob
blurb: Roasted, slightly charred corn without boiling a giant pot of water in August.
shake: Roll each ear a half-turn at 6 minutes.
internalNote: Done when kernels are plump, bright yellow, and lightly charred in spots.
prep: Husk completely and remove all silk. Snap ears in half if they don't fit your basket.
tips: Butter after cooking, not before — butter burns and smokes at 390°F.
Halve the ears to fit and to get more surface contact with the basket.
For elote, brush with mayo-crema mix in the final 2 minutes then top with cotija and chili.
steps: Husk corn and remove all silk; halve ears if needed to fit.
Rub lightly with oil and salt.
Arrange in a single layer, not stacked.
Cook at 390°F for 6 minutes, roll, then 6 more minutes.
Top with butter, chili powder and lime off the heat.

faq.q: Can I cook corn in the husk?
faq.a: Yes — 390°F for about 15 minutes. The husk steams the kernels, giving a softer, sweeter result with no char.
390°F for 16 minutes, rolling twice. It's already blanched, so you're mostly heating and browning it.

name: Mushrooms
blurb: Mushrooms release a lot of water, then brown fast once it's gone. The air fryer moves through both stages quicker than a skillet.
shake: Shake at 6 minutes, right around when the released water has evaporated.
internalNote: Done when browned, shrunk by roughly a third, and no liquid remains in the basket.
prep: Wipe clean with a damp cloth rather than rinsing. Mushrooms are sponges and soaked ones never brown.
tips: Don't salt until the last 3 minutes — early salt draws out water and prolongs the steaming phase.
Halve or quarter them; whole mushrooms take twice as long to release their water.
Butter and garlic go in at the end, once the water has cooked off.
steps: Wipe mushrooms clean and halve them.
Toss with oil only — no salt yet.
Cook at 380°F for 6 minutes.
Shake, add garlic, butter, salt and pepper, then cook 6 more minutes.
Toss with thyme and serve.

faq.a: Salted too early, or crowded. Salt at the end and cook in a single loose layer so the released steam can escape.
370°F for 10 minutes. Use large portobello or stuffing-size caps and don't overfill, or the filling spills as they shrink.

name: Carrots
blurb: Roasting concentrates carrot sugars into something almost candied. Air frying does it in half the oven's time.
shake: Shake at 8 minutes.
internalNote: Done when caramelized at the edges and a fork slides through with light pressure.
prep: Cut into uniform sticks or coins about 1/2-inch thick. Whole baby carrots work but stay firmer in the center.
tips: Add honey or maple only in the last 4 minutes — sugar burns quickly at 380°F.
Uniform thickness matters more than shape. Mixed sizes give you burnt thin bits and raw thick ones.
Cumin, coriander and a pinch of chili work better with carrots than sweet glaze alone.
steps: Peel and cut carrots into even sticks.
Toss with oil, salt, cumin and pepper.
Cook at 380°F for 8 minutes.
Shake and cook 4 more minutes.
Drizzle with honey and cook a final 4 minutes; garnish with parsley.

faq.a: Baby carrots need about 18 minutes and stay firmer because of their thickness. Cut sticks caramelize better thanks to the flat cut faces.
380°F for 20 minutes. They come out tender rather than caramelized because of surface moisture.

name: Crispy Tofu
blurb: The air fryer solves tofu. No shallow-frying, no sticking to the pan, and every single cube gets a golden crust.
shake: Shake at 8 minutes to rotate the cubes.
internalNote: Done when cubes are golden on multiple faces and firm-springy when pressed.
prep: Press extra-firm tofu for at least 20 minutes under something heavy. Then toss cubes with cornstarch — this is what creates the crust.
tips: Extra-firm only. Silken or soft tofu disintegrates in the basket.
One tablespoon of cornstarch per block is the difference between crispy and merely warm.
Sauce it after cooking. Marinating wet tofu before air frying prevents any crust from forming.
ingredients: 14 oz extra-firm tofu, pressed and cubed
steps: Press tofu 20 minutes, then cut into 1-inch cubes.
Toss cubes with soy sauce, then with oil.
Dust with cornstarch and garlic powder, tossing until evenly coated.
Cook at 390°F for 8 minutes in a single layer.
Shake and cook 7 more minutes until golden; finish with sesame oil.

faq.q: Do I have to press tofu?
faq.a: For crispy results, yes. Water in the block turns to steam and prevents any surface browning. Twenty minutes under a heavy pan is enough.
Freeze and thaw it first — this creates a spongier, chewier texture that many people prefer. Press hard after thawing, then cook as usual.

name: Falafel
blurb: Deep-fried texture without a liter of oil. Air-fried falafel is drier inside than fried, so a generous oil spray matters.
shake: Shake at 7 minutes.
internalNote: Done when deeply golden outside and steaming-hot through the center.
prep: Use soaked dried chickpeas, never canned — canned chickpeas hold too much water and the mixture won't hold together.
tips: Dried soaked chickpeas only. Canned falafel mix falls apart in the basket, every time.
Spray generously with oil on all sides; unoiled falafel comes out chalky.
Chill the shaped balls 30 minutes before cooking so they hold their shape.
steps: Pulse soaked chickpeas with onion, garlic and herbs to a coarse crumb — not a puree.
Mix in spices, salt and flour; chill 30 minutes.
Form into 12 balls and flatten slightly.
Spray all sides generously with oil.
Cook at 375°F for 7 minutes, shake, then 7 more minutes until deep golden.

faq.q: Why did my falafel fall apart?
faq.a: Canned chickpeas, or the mixture was over-processed into a paste. Use soaked dried chickpeas and pulse only to a coarse crumb.
375°F for about 12 minutes, shaking once. No thawing and no oil needed — they're pre-fried.

name: Halloumi
blurb: A cheese that holds its shape under heat. Eight minutes gives you a golden crust and a squeaky, molten center.
shake: Flip pieces at 4 minutes with tongs.
internalNote: Done when golden-brown on the cut faces and soft when pressed.
prep: Pat very dry and cut into 1/2-inch slabs or thick fries. Wet halloumi steams and stays pale.
tips: Halloumi is already salty — don't add salt, only pepper or herbs.
Serve immediately. It firms into rubber within about five minutes of cooling.
A light dust of cornstarch makes halloumi fries genuinely crunchy.
ingredients: 1 block halloumi (8-9 oz), cut into fries
steps: Pat halloumi very dry and cut into thick fries.
Toss lightly with oil, cornstarch and oregano.
Arrange in a single layer with gaps.
Cook at 380°F for 4 minutes, flip, then 4 more.
Serve immediately with honey and lemon.

faq.q: Will halloumi melt in the air fryer?
faq.a: No. Halloumi has a high melting point and holds its shape — that's what makes it work here where mozzarella would collapse.

faq.q: Can I cook it from frozen?
faq.a: Thaw first. Frozen halloumi releases water as it thaws in the basket and steams instead of browning.

name: Crispy Chickpeas
blurb: A genuinely crunchy high-protein snack for pennies. The trick is drying them properly and accepting they crisp fully only as they cool.
shake: Shake at 7 minutes, and again at 12 if you're doing a full basket.
internalNote: Done when they rattle in the basket and a test chickpea crunches rather than yields.
prep: Drain, rinse, then dry hard between towels. Rub off any loose skins — they burn before the chickpea crisps.
tips: They finish crisping as they cool. Don't judge them straight out of the basket.
Season after cooking for maximum crunch; spices added early absorb moisture and go soft.
Store in an open bowl, never a sealed container — trapped steam turns them chewy overnight.
ingredients: 2 cans chickpeas (15 oz each), drained and dried
steps: Drain, rinse and dry chickpeas thoroughly; remove loose skins.
Toss with oil only.
Cook at 390°F for 7 minutes.
Shake and cook 8 more minutes until rattly and hard.
Toss with the spice blend immediately, then cool 10 minutes to finish crisping.

faq.q: Why are mine chewy, not crunchy?
faq.a: Not dry enough before cooking, or stored airtight afterward. Dry them hard and leave them uncovered after cooking.
They're best within a few hours. After a day they soften noticeably — a 3-minute re-crisp at 390°F brings them back.

name: Cookies
blurb: Six cookies in eight minutes with no oven preheat. Air fryer cookies spread less and stay chewier in the middle than oven-baked.
shake: No shake or flip. Rotate the parchment 180° at 5 minutes if your model browns unevenly.
internalNote: Pull when edges are set and centers still look slightly underdone — they firm up on the rack.
prep: Cut parchment to size and place cookies with 2 inches between them. Let the parchment be weighed down by the dough before the fan starts, or it will fly into the element.
tips: 320°F, much lower than oven temperature. The fan is aggressive and 350°F burns cookie tops before centers set.
Never put empty parchment in a preheating air fryer — it can lift into the heating element. Always weigh it down with dough.
Underbake slightly. Residual heat finishes them and you get a chewy center.
steps: Cream butter and sugars, then beat in egg and vanilla.
Fold in flour, baking soda, salt and chocolate chips.
Place 6 dough balls on parchment cut to fit the basket, 2 inches apart.
Cook at 320°F for 8 minutes until edges are set.
Cool on the parchment 5 minutes before moving — they're fragile when hot.

faq.q: Can I bake frozen cookie dough?
faq.a: Yes. 320°F for about 11 minutes straight from frozen. Frozen dough actually spreads less, which many people prefer.

faq.q: Why did my cookies burn on top?
faq.a: Temperature too high or the rack sits too close to the element. Drop to 310°F and check at 6 minutes.

name: Donuts
blurb: Canned biscuit dough turns into passable donuts in five minutes. They're more like fried biscuits than yeast donuts, and they're excellent.
shake: Flip at 3 minutes with tongs.
internalNote: Done when golden on both sides and no raw dough remains — split one to check the first time.
prep: Separate the biscuits and cut a 1-inch hole from the center of each with a bottle cap or small cutter. Cook the holes too.
tips: Brush with melted butter the moment they come out so cinnamon sugar sticks.
Don't skip cutting the center hole — solid rounds stay doughy in the middle.
Glaze only after they've cooled 5 minutes, or it slides straight off.
steps: Separate biscuits and cut a 1-inch hole in each center.
Spray the basket and both sides of the dough lightly with oil.
Cook at 350°F for 3 minutes, flip, then 3 more minutes.
Brush hot donuts with melted butter.
Toss in combined cinnamon sugar and serve warm.

faq.a: Yes, but they need a full proof and come out drier than fried. Cook at 350°F for 6 minutes and brush generously with butter.
350°F for about 9 minutes from frozen, flipping halfway.

name: Reheating Leftover Pizza
blurb: The single best use of an air fryer that nobody mentions in the manual. Three minutes restores a crisp base a microwave can never produce.
shake: No flip needed.
internalNote: Reheat leftovers to 165°F throughout, per USDA guidance for previously cooked food.
prep: None. Straight from the fridge into the basket.
tips: 350°F, not higher. Hot air hits the cheese first and 400°F browns the toppings before the base warms.
Lay slices flat, not overlapping. Overlap creates a soggy seam.
A tiny sprinkle of water on the crust before reheating steams it soft, then the air crisps it — bakery trick.
steps: Place slices flat in the basket without overlapping.
Cook at 350°F for 3 minutes.
Check the cheese; add 1 more minute if needed.
Serve immediately.

faq.a: No. Stacking traps steam and you get a soft, floppy crust — exactly what you were trying to avoid.
350°F for about 6 minutes straight from frozen. There's no need to thaw.

name: Reheating Leftover Fries
blurb: Day-old fries genuinely come back to life. Three minutes at high heat drives off the moisture that made them limp.
shake: Shake at 2 minutes — with a 3-minute cook, that one shake does most of the work.
internalNote: Heat leftovers through to 165°F. For fries this happens well before they re-crisp.
prep: Spread them out. Cold fries clump in the container and clumped fries reheat unevenly.
tips: High heat, short time. 400°F for 3 minutes; longer just dries them into sticks.
A very light oil spray helps if they were originally baked rather than fried.
Never microwave first. Once fries go soft from steam, no amount of air frying fully rescues them.
steps: Break up any clumps and spread fries in a loose layer.
Cook at 400°F for 2 minutes.
Shake the basket.
Cook 1 more minute until hot and crisp; salt lightly and serve.

faq.a: Usually not — restaurant fries carry enough residual fat. A light spray helps home-baked fries that started out low-fat.
Two to three days refrigerated is fine. Beyond that the potato texture degrades in ways reheating can't fix.

name: Hard "Boiled" Eggs
blurb: No water, no pot, no watching for a boil. And they peel more easily than pot-boiled eggs, which is the real selling point.
shake: No shake. Eggs crack if they roll into each other.
internalNote: 15 minutes at 270°F gives a fully set yolk. 11 minutes gives a jammy center; 13 gives a soft-set yolk.
prep: Nothing. Place eggs straight from the fridge into the basket.
tips: Ice bath immediately after cooking. It stops the cooking and makes the shell release cleanly.
Every air fryer differs by a minute or two — test one egg first and note your model's timing.
Brown spots on the shell are harmless contact marks from the basket, not burns.
steps: Place eggs directly in the basket in a single layer, not touching.
Cook at 270°F for 15 minutes.
Transfer immediately to an ice water bath for 5 minutes.
Peel under running water for the cleanest release.

faq.a: No, as long as you stay at 270°F or below and use a proper ice bath afterward. Higher temperatures can crack shells.
11 minutes at 270°F gives a runny-jammy yolk; 13 minutes gives a soft-set center. Ice bath immediately either way.

name: Toast & Garlic Bread
blurb: When you need four slices at once and your toaster only holds two. Also the best method for frozen garlic bread by a wide margin.
shake: Flip at 2 minutes for even browning on both faces.
internalNote: Done at your preferred shade of golden. Check at 3 minutes the first time — bread goes from pale to burnt fast.
prep: None for plain toast. For garlic bread, spread butter mixture edge to edge so the corners don't scorch.
tips: Light bread can lift into the heating element from the fan. Weigh slices down with a rack or a heavier topping.
Check at 3 minutes. Bread browns unpredictably between models.
For garlic bread, add cheese only in the last 2 minutes so it melts without burning.
steps: Arrange bread in a single layer.
For garlic bread, spread the butter-garlic mixture edge to edge first.
Cook at 370°F for 2 minutes.
Flip plain toast, or add cheese to garlic bread.
Cook 2 more minutes until golden.

faq.q: Why did my bread fly around?
faq.a: The fan lifts light slices. Place a metal rack on top, or butter the bread to weigh it down.
370°F for about 6 minutes straight from frozen — no thawing. It beats the oven both on time and on crust.

name: Frozen Egg Rolls
blurb: Blistered, bubbly wrappers that taste deep-fried. Frozen egg rolls are one of the highest-return items in the freezer aisle for air fryer owners.
shake: Roll each one a half-turn at 6 minutes using tongs.
internalNote: Frozen egg rolls are pre-cooked; reheat to 165°F throughout. Check that the filling center is steaming, not cold.
prep: No thawing. A light oil spray gives a more even blistered finish on the wrapper.
tips: Space them so no two wrappers touch — contact points stay pale and soft.
Spray lightly with oil for the bubbly, deep-fried look.
Mini egg rolls need only 8 minutes; check them early.
steps: Arrange frozen egg rolls in a single layer with gaps between.
Spray lightly with oil.
Cook at 390°F for 6 minutes.
Turn each roll a half-turn and cook 6 more minutes.
Rest 2 minutes — the filling is extremely hot.

faq.q: Do I thaw egg rolls first?
faq.a: Never. Thawed wrappers go soggy and can split open in the basket, spilling filling.
390°F for 10 minutes, turning halfway. Brush the wrappers with oil or they stay dry and papery.

name: Frozen Dumplings & Potstickers
blurb: Crisp bottoms without the pan-fry-then-steam dance. You lose a bit of the pillowy top, but you gain a whole-surface crunch.
shake: Shake gently at 6 minutes — dumpling skins tear if you're rough.
internalNote: 165°F. Filling with raw pork or chicken must reach this temperature; cut one open to confirm on your first batch.
prep: Spray both the basket and the dumplings with oil. Dumpling skins stick to bare metal more than almost any other food.
tips: Oil the basket, not just the food. Skins weld to dry metal and tear when you lift them.
For a softer top, brush the dumplings with water at the halfway shake.
Don't overlap. Touching dumplings fuse into one mass.
steps: Spray the basket with oil, then arrange dumplings without touching.
Spray the tops lightly with oil.
Cook at 380°F for 6 minutes.
Shake gently, brush with a little water if you want softer skins.
Cook 6 more minutes until bottoms are golden and crisp.

faq.q: Can I cook soup dumplings this way?
faq.a: No. Xiao long bao need gentle steam; hot dry air ruptures the skin and you lose the soup entirely.
Dry basket. Always spray the basket surface itself, or use perforated parchment.

name: Frozen Burritos
blurb: A microwave gives you a soggy tube with a lava core and a frozen center. The air fryer gives you a crisp tortilla and even heat.
shake: Turn each burrito over at 9 minutes.
internalNote: 165°F at the center. This is the food people most often serve still frozen inside — check the middle with a thermometer or a knife.
prep: Remove all plastic wrapping. Leave the burrito whole and unwrapped.
tips: 350°F, not 400°F. A burrito is dense; high heat scorches the tortilla long before the center thaws.
If the tortilla browns too fast, wrap loosely in foil for the first 10 minutes then unwrap to crisp.
Let it rest 3 minutes after cooking — the filling heat equalizes and stops it burning your mouth.
ingredients: Salsa and sour cream, to serve
steps: Unwrap burritos completely and place seam-side down.
Cook at 350°F for 9 minutes.
Turn each burrito over.
Cook 9 more minutes until the tortilla is crisp and the center reads 165°F.
Rest 3 minutes before eating.

faq.q: Why is the middle still cold?
faq.a: Temperature too high, time too short. Drop to 350°F and give it the full 18 minutes — dense frozen food needs time, not heat.

faq.q: Can I air fry a fresh burrito?
faq.a: Yes. 380°F for 12 minutes, seam-side down first, gives you a crisp restaurant-style shell.

name: Apple Chips
blurb: Low and slow, closer to dehydrating than frying. Twenty-five minutes gives you crisp, naturally sweet chips with zero added sugar.
shake: Flip the slices at 12 minutes — they curl and stick otherwise.
internalNote: Done when slices are dry to the touch and lightly leathery; they crisp fully as they cool.
prep: Slice as thinly and evenly as possible — a mandoline at 1/8 inch is ideal. Thick slices stay chewy.
tips: Thin and even is everything. Uneven slices give you burnt edges and damp centers in the same batch.
They crisp as they cool, so don't extend the time based on how they feel hot.
A pinch of cinnamon before cooking, not sugar — sugar burns at this length of cook.
steps: Core apples and slice into 1/8-inch rounds.
Toss with lemon juice to prevent browning, then pat dry.
Dust with cinnamon.
Arrange in a single layer — overlap is unavoidable in small baskets, so plan two batches.
Cook at 300°F for 12 minutes, flip, then 13 more minutes.
Cool completely on a rack to finish crisping.

faq.a: Sliced too thick or not cooled properly. Aim for 1/8 inch and let them cool fully on a rack before judging.

faq.q: Can I use a lower temperature?
faq.a: Yes — 250°F for 45 minutes gives more evenly dehydrated chips if your model goes that low.

name: Kale Chips
blurb: Five minutes and the lightest crisp in the kitchen. The whole challenge is stopping the leaves from flying into the heating element.
shake: Shake at 3 minutes, briefly — the leaves are fragile once dry.
internalNote: Done when leaves are dry, crackly and still deep green. Brown means burnt and bitter.
prep: Strip leaves from the tough stems, wash, and dry completely in a salad spinner. Wet kale steams into slime.
tips: Place a metal rack over the kale to stop the fan launching leaves into the element — this is a real fire-safety point.
320°F maximum. Kale burns and turns bitter above that in under a minute.
Massage the oil into the leaves by hand so every surface is coated with a very thin film.
steps: Strip and tear kale into palm-size pieces; wash and dry completely.
Massage oil into the leaves until barely glossy.
Add to the basket and place a metal rack on top to hold them down.
Cook at 320°F for 3 minutes, shake, then 2 more minutes.
Season with salt and nutritional yeast once out of the basket.

faq.q: My kale flew into the heating element — is that dangerous?
faq.a: It can smoke or scorch. Always weigh the leaves down with a rack or trivet; this is the most common air fryer safety complaint with leafy greens.
Overcooked. Kale goes from crisp to burnt in about 45 seconds. Drop to 300°F and check every minute near the end.

name: Frozen Fish Sticks
blurb: Ten minutes, no flipping stress, and a crunch the oven can't match. A weeknight staple with essentially zero failure rate.
shake: Shake at 5 minutes.
internalNote: 165°F. Fish sticks are pre-cooked but must be reheated fully; the center should be steaming hot.
prep: None. Straight from the freezer, no oil needed.
tips: No oil and no thawing — the coating is already par-fried.
A single layer browns best, but two layers work if you shake twice.
Add 2 minutes for the thicker battered fillet style versus thin fish fingers.
ingredients: Tartar sauce and lemon, to serve
steps: Arrange fish sticks in the basket, roughly level.
Cook at 400°F for 5 minutes.
Shake the basket.
Cook 5 more minutes until golden and crisp.
Serve with tartar sauce and lemon.

faq.a: Not required, though 3 minutes of preheat gives a crisper coating. Add a minute if you skip it.
Two layers is fine with two shakes. Three layers steams the middle.

name: Jalapeño Poppers
blurb: Golden coating, molten center, no deep fryer. The main risk is cheese leaking out — which lower heat and a watchful timer prevent.
shake: Turn each popper with tongs at 5 minutes rather than shaking.
internalNote: 165°F for poppers containing bacon or meat. For plain cheese poppers, golden coating and molten filling is the cue.
prep: For homemade: halve jalapeños, remove seeds and membrane, fill with cream cheese, then bread. Chill the breaded poppers 30 minutes so the coating sets.
tips: Place them filling-side up so the cheese has less chance to escape.
375°F maximum for frozen — hotter and the cheese blows out before the breading colors.
Wear gloves when seeding jalapeños, and don't touch your eyes afterward.
ingredients: 10 frozen jalapeño poppers, or 5 fresh jalapeños
steps: Arrange poppers filling-side up in a single layer with gaps.
Spray lightly with oil.
Cook at 375°F for 5 minutes.
Turn each popper carefully with tongs.
Cook 4 more minutes until golden; rest 2 minutes before eating.

faq.q: Why did the cheese leak out?
faq.a: Too hot or too long. Drop to 370°F, cut a minute, and keep them filling-side up throughout.
370°F for 12 minutes. Chill the breaded poppers 30 minutes first so the coating firms up and seals the filling.

name: Frozen Hash Browns
blurb: Crisper than a skillet and no flipping half a pound of shredded potato with a spatula. Patties in particular come out perfect every time.
serving: 4 hash brown patties or 1 lb shredded
shake: Flip patties at 6 minutes; shake shredded hash browns instead.
internalNote: Done when deep golden and rigid. Shredded hash browns should have crisp edges and no pale damp clumps.
prep: No thawing. For shredded, break up any frozen clumps before they go in so they cook evenly.
tips: Patties need no oil at all; shredded benefits from a light spray to help the strands separate and brown.
Single layer for patties — stacked ones steam and stay pale in the middle.
Add 2 minutes for genuinely crunchy edges rather than merely cooked.
ingredients: 4 frozen hash brown patties, or 1 lb frozen shredded hash browns
steps: Place patties in a single layer, or spread shredded hash browns in a loose 1-inch layer.
Cook at 400°F for 6 minutes.
Flip patties or shake shredded potatoes thoroughly.
Cook 6 more minutes until deep golden.
Season and serve immediately.

faq.q: Why are shredded hash browns pale in the middle?
faq.a: The layer was too deep or you didn't shake. Keep it under an inch and shake at least once — twice is better.

faq.q: Can I make them from fresh potato?
faq.a: Yes. Shred, rinse off the starch, and squeeze bone-dry in a towel. Then 400°F for 14 minutes with a light oil spray, shaking twice.
